title: Point of view and perspective
blurb: Name the narrator's point of view from the narration (not the dialogue), and read an author's perspective from word choice, emphasis and what is left out.
question: A story opens, “‘I can't do this,’ Jamal muttered,” and then describes what Ms. Reyes, watching from the doorway, remembers and decides. Is the story told in first person or third person, and whose perspective shapes it?

teach.body: On the TEAS, point of view has two meanings. Narrative point of view is who tells the story and how much the narrator knows: first, second or third person. Perspective is the author's position or attitude toward the topic: supportive, opposed, neutral, skeptical and so on. Plain English: point of view asks “Who is talking, and what can they see?” Perspective asks “Where does the writer stand?”

head: Point of view
Pronouns
Narrator knows
teach.caption: Second person is common in instructions and some ads (“Bring your ID”).

root.label: Read the narration, skip the quotes

teach.caption: Pronouns inside quotation marks belong to the speaker, not the narrator.

teach.h: Scenario: Hannah reads a story excerpt
teach.body: Hannah, a nursing applicant, reads: “‘I can't do this,’ Jamal muttered, staring at the beeping IV pump. Ms. Reyes watched him from the doorway. She remembered her own first week on the floor, when every alarm had sounded like a disaster. She decided to wait a moment before stepping in. Jamal pressed the silence button and, frowning, began to trace the tubing with one finger.”

teach.h: How Hannah names the point of view
items: Set aside the dialogue: “I can't do this” is Jamal speaking, not the narrator.
Check the narration's pronouns: “she,” “him,” “her.” So it is third person.
Whose thoughts do we get? Ms. Reyes “remembered” and “decided.”
Jamal's thoughts? Only his words and actions (muttered, frowned, traced): we never enter his mind.
One character's inner thoughts: third person limited, from Ms. Reyes's perspective.

teach.body: An author's perspective is shaped by background, role and purpose: a hospital administrator, a patient and a nurse may all write about staffing and stress different things. Find it from word choice (connotation), what is emphasized, what is left out, and tone. Writing can be objective (neutral, balanced, factual, usually third person) or subjective (personal, opinionated). Statistics do not make a text objective if the words around them are slanted.

teach.caption: Ambivalent is different from neutral: an ambivalent author has mixed feelings and sees real pros and cons.

head: Writer's role
Likely emphasis
teach.caption: Ask who the writer is and what they would naturally stress or leave out.

teach.text: Four classic traps: using pronouns inside quoted dialogue to name the point of view; giving the author the views of an opponent the author quotes in order to rebut; calling a passage neutral because it contains statistics while its word choice is clearly slanted; and confusing tone (the author's attitude) with mood (the reader's feeling) or with the topic.

items: First person: I/we, narrator is a character. Second person: you.
Third limited: one character's thoughts. Omniscient: all characters'. Objective: actions and words only.
Ignore pronouns inside quotation marks when naming the point of view.
Perspective comes from word choice, emphasis, omissions, tone and the writer's role.
Separate the author's own view from views the author reports or rebuts.

summary: You can now identify first, second and third person (limited, omniscient and objective) narration without being fooled by dialogue. You can also determine an author's perspective from word choice, emphasis and role, keeping it separate from views the author reports.

A.q: “You'll want to arrive at the testing center fifteen minutes early. Bring your photo ID, and leave your phone in your car.” From which point of view is this passage written?
A.why: The passage addresses the reader directly as “you,” which is second person, the usual choice for instructions.

whyNot.2: No character is described as “he” or “she,” and no one's thoughts are given.
whyNot.3: Third person objective reports characters' actions; this text speaks directly to the reader.

A.q: “I watched Grandma Rose fold her napkin into a perfect square. She had told the story of her nursing-school graduation a hundred times, and she told it again now, her eyes bright.” From which point of view is this passage written?
A.why: The narrator is a character in the scene who says “I watched.” That makes it first person, even though most pronouns refer to Grandma Rose.

whyNot.0: Many pronouns are “she,” but they describe Grandma Rose; the narrator is an “I.”
whyNot.1: The narrator is a participant using “I,” not an outside voice that knows every character's mind.
whyNot.3: The reader is never addressed as “you.”

A.q: “Critics call the hospital's new open-visiting policy chaotic. Yet since it began, patient satisfaction scores have climbed, and nurses report that families now help with meals and mobility.” Which best describes the author's perspective on the policy?
options: The author agrees it is chaotic
The author is neutral about it
The author wants it to be revised
A.why: The author reports the critics' view and answers it with “Yet” and positive evidence. The author's own perspective is supportive.

whyNot.1: “Chaotic” is the critics' word, which the author reports in order to rebut.
whyNot.2: Only favorable evidence follows “Yet,” so the author takes a side.
whyNot.3: The passage defends the policy as it stands and proposes no changes.

B.q: “Dr. Kim hoped the test results would be clear enough to share. Across the room, Mrs. Alvarez wondered whether she should have called her daughter. Neither of them noticed the storm clouds gathering outside.” From which point of view is this passage written?
B.why: The narrator reveals what both Dr. Kim (“hoped”) and Mrs. Alvarez (“wondered”) are thinking, and what neither notices. Knowing several characters' minds is third person omniscient.

whyNot.0: Limited narration stays inside one character's mind; this enters two.
whyNot.1: Objective narration reports only actions and words, not hopes and wonderings.
whyNot.2: No narrator takes part in the scene as an “I.”

B.q: “The nurse entered the room and set the tray on the table. ‘Morning,’ she said. The patient did not answer. He turned toward the window and pulled the blanket to his chin.” From which point of view is this passage written?
B.why: The narrator reports only what can be seen and heard (entering, speaking, turning) and never reveals anyone's thoughts. That is third person objective.

whyNot.1: Limited narration would reveal one character's thoughts or feelings; none are given.
whyNot.2: Omniscient narration would reveal several characters' thoughts; none are given.

B.q: Several people write opinion pieces about hiring more nurses at a city hospital. Whose piece would most likely focus on the cost of the new salaries?
options: A patient waiting in the ER
A family member of a patient
B.why: A writer's role shapes perspective. The finance chief is responsible for budgets, so salary costs are the natural emphasis.

whyNot.0: A waiting patient would most likely stress wait times and attention.
whyNot.1: A nurse on double shifts would most likely stress workload and rest.
whyNot.3: A family member would most likely stress care quality and communication.

C.q: “The district's new 8:45 start time has drawn complaints from some parents about morning child care, and their frustration is understandable. But consider the district's own data: first-period absences fell 18 percent last semester, and late arrivals dropped by nearly a third. Teenagers, it turns out, learn better when they are not sleepwalking through algebra. A few rearranged carpools seem a small price to pay.” Which best describes the author's perspective?
options: Neutral, since it reports district data
C.why: The author acknowledges parents' frustration but answers it with “But consider,” favorable data and dismissive phrases (“a small price to pay”). The perspective is supportive with a concession.

whyNot.0: The statistics are framed by slanted words (“sleepwalking,” “a small price”), so the passage is not neutral.
whyNot.1: The child-care complaint belongs to some parents; the author concedes it, then argues past it.
whyNot.3: The sides are not weighed equally: the concession takes one clause, and the rest argues for the change.

C.q: “‘We're going to be late again,’ Tasha's brother groaned from the back seat. Tasha gripped the wheel and told herself the traffic would clear by the next exit; she could not afford another late mark at her clinical site. Beside her, their mother hummed along to the radio.” From which point of view is the passage narrated?
C.why: The narration uses “she” and “her” and reveals only Tasha's thoughts (what she told herself, what she could not afford). The brother's words and the mother's humming are reported from outside. That is third person limited.

whyNot.0: “We're” appears only inside the brother's quoted words; the narrator never says “I” or “we.”
whyNot.1: The narrator does not enter the brother's or the mother's mind, so it is not omniscient.
whyNot.2: The reader is never addressed as “you.”

C.q: A reporter is writing an objective news article about a clinic's extended hours. Which sentence fits that purpose best?
options: At last, the clinic is listening to working families.
The clinic now stays open until 9 p.m. on weekdays.
Sadly, the new hours will probably be cut next year.
Patients surely agree the new hours are a gift.
C.why: An objective sentence reports a checkable fact in neutral words. Stating the new closing time does that.

whyNot.0: “At last” and “listening to working families” express the writer's approval, which is subjective.
whyNot.2: “Sadly” reveals a feeling, and “probably” is a guess about the future.
whyNot.3: “Surely” and “a gift” express opinion and assume what all patients think.

reteach.title: Where is the camera?
reteach.question: Imagine filming a scene in a busy hospital hallway. Where you put the camera, and whether it can hear thoughts, is the point of view.

blocks.body: Strap the camera to one nurse's forehead and let her narrate: first person. Point the camera at the viewer and give instructions: second person. Follow one nurse from behind with a microphone that picks up her thoughts: third limited. Use a drone that hears every character's thoughts: third omniscient. Use a security camera with no thought microphone, just actions and words: third objective.

blocks.text: A character shouting “I” into the security camera does not turn it into a forehead camera. Dialogue pronouns never change the narrator's point of view.

explain.body: First person: the narrator is a character using I, me, we, my. Second person: the text speaks to the reader as you, typical of instructions and some ads.

test.q: “We reached the clinic just after dawn. My sister held the paperwork while I parked, and we joined a line that already wrapped around the building.” From which point of view is this passage written?
test.why: The narrator takes part in the events and uses “we,” “my” and “I.” That is first person.

whyNot.0: The reader is not addressed as “you.”
whyNot.1: The narrator is a participant, not an outside voice using “he” or “she.”
whyNot.2: The narration is told by an “I” inside the scene, not by a detached observer.

explain.body: All use he, she, they. Limited: the narrator knows one character's thoughts. Omniscient: the narrator knows every character's thoughts. Objective: the narrator reports only actions and words, like a camera.

test.q: “Marcus scanned the waiting room, hoping no one would notice how nervous he was. The receptionist called a name. A woman by the window stood, gathered her coat and walked toward the desk.” From which point of view is this passage written?
test.why: The narrator reveals Marcus's hope and nervousness but reports only the actions of the receptionist and the woman. One character's thoughts means third person limited.

whyNot.0: Omniscient narration would also reveal the woman's or the receptionist's thoughts.
whyNot.2: Objective narration would not reveal Marcus's hope or nervousness.

explain.body: Perspective is the author's position on the topic: opposed, skeptical, neutral, ambivalent, supportive or enthusiastic. Find it from word choice, emphasis, what is left out, and tone.

test.q: “The company insists its new smartwatch can ‘detect heart problems before your doctor can.’ The watch does record heart rate. Whether it catches problems earlier than a checkup is another matter, and the company has released no study to show it.” Which phrase best reveals the author's skeptical perspective?
test.why: “Is another matter” signals the author's doubt about the company's claim, which the missing study then reinforces.

whyNot.1: This states what the watch actually does; it is a neutral fact the author accepts.
whyNot.2: This simply names the product without judging it.
whyNot.3: These are the company's words, quoted by the author, not the author's own view.

explain.body: Authors often quote experts or opponents. A quoted view belongs to the speaker. Look for a turn (but, yet, however, in fact) and the evidence that follows it to find the author's own position.

test.q: “Some residents say the downtown farmers market brings only traffic and noise. In fact, a city survey found that nearby shops earn more on market days, and the market's 40 vendors pay fees that fund street cleaning.” Which view belongs to the author?
options: The market mostly brings traffic and noise
The city should move the market elsewhere
The market benefits the downtown area
The vendors' fees are set too high
test.why: After “In fact,” the author offers evidence of benefits to shops and street cleaning. The author's view is that the market helps downtown.

whyNot.0: This is the view of “some residents,” which the author reports in order to rebut.
whyNot.1: No relocation is proposed; the author defends the market where it is.
whyNot.3: The fees are mentioned as a benefit, not criticized.
